Chapter 7: The Power of Information and the Challenge of Denial
Change really does start with something simple—just learning something new.
But have you ever noticed? Just knowing the facts rarely changes everything. The truth about animal suffering, for example, is out there for anyone to see. There are books, documentaries, news stories—countless ways to understand what happens in factory farms or animal testing labs. And yet, for so many people, those facts just... bounce right off. Hardly a dent.
The real challenge isn’t just not knowing. It’s denial.
Picture this: a family at dinner. Someone brings up a news story about cruelty on a local farm. Suddenly, there’s an awkward silence. Maybe someone quickly changes the subject. That discomfort is real, but let’s be honest—it’s easier to brush it aside than to actually face what it might mean. Most of us want to see ourselves as good people. The thought that our everyday choices could cause harm? That’s a tough pill to swallow.
Denial shows up in all kinds of ways. Sometimes, it’s flat-out disbelief—“There’s no way it’s really that bad.” Other times, it’s rationalizing—“Animals probably don’t feel pain like we do,” or “That’s just the way the world works.” And honestly, a lot of the time, it’s just not thinking about it at all. If the suffering is out of sight, it’s easy for it to stay out of mind.
But here’s the thing—information has this quiet persistence. It seeps in, especially when it comes from someone we trust. Maybe it’s a friend who gently shares why they stopped eating meat. Or a teacher assigning a book that makes us question old habits. Sometimes, it’s even a child asking, “Why do we eat some animals but not others?”
Those little moments—they can crack open the walls of denial, and that’s when change starts to feel possible.
The real power of information isn’t just in the facts. It’s in the stories that make those facts come alive. When we see the world through someone else’s eyes—human or animal—compassion actually has a chance. That’s why it matters to keep telling these stories, to keep asking those uncomfortable questions, and to refuse to let suffering stay hidden in the shadows.
For a lot of people, moving past denial is slow. It’s so much easier to laugh off the discomfort, or hope someone else will fix things. But every single time the truth is faced—even for a moment—the possibility for change grows a little bit stronger.
So next time you come across a tough fact, try not to turn away right away. That uncomfortable feeling? It means something matters. And honestly, that’s often where real change begins.
